introduction-from-dead-metal-to-live-sys.core: Booting is a relay. Firmware (BIOS or UEFI) initialises hardware and finds a bootloader; the bootloader (GRUB) loads the kernel and initramfs; the kernel initialises memory, CPUs and drivers; the initramfs finds and mounts the real root filesystem; and PID 1 (systemd) starts services to reach the target. Knowing each handoff tells you where a boot failure is and what tool can fix it.

first_principles.problem: A server doesn't come back after a reboot, and the team doesn't know whether to look at BIOS, GRUB, the kernel or systemd.
truths: Each stage hands off to the next.

analogy.title: A relay race
analogy.story: Each runner passes the baton; if it's dropped, you know which handoff failed.
analogy.breaks: Relay runners are visible; boot stages are only visible on console.

check.q: If boot drops to a dracut emergency shell, which stage failed?
check.a: The initramfs stage, typically failing to find or mount the real root filesystem.

stage-1-the-hardware-handshake-bios-vs-u.core: Legacy BIOS runs POST, then reads the first 512-byte sector (MBR) of the boot disk and executes it, which has tiny space, limited partition tables and 2 TB disks. UEFI is modern firmware that understands GPT partitions and FAT filesystems: it loads .efi bootloaders from the EFI System Partition, stores boot entries in NVRAM (efibootmgr), supports Secure Boot signature verification, and offers network and HTTP boot. Cloud VMs and modern servers use UEFI.

first_principles.problem: A cloned disk won't boot on a new server because it was set up for legacy BIOS and the server is UEFI-only.
truths: UEFI reads filesystems and verifies signatures.

analogy.title: A guard reading the first page vs a librarian with a catalogue
analogy.story: The old guard only reads the first page of the first book; the librarian finds the right book by title and checks its seal.
analogy.breaks: Librarians can be persuaded; Secure Boot strictly checks signatures.

code.text:
[ -d /sys/firmware/efi ] && echo UEFI || echo BIOS
efibootmgr -v | head
# Boot0001* ubuntu  HD(1,GPT,...)/File(\EFI\ubuntu\shimx64.efi)
mokutil --sb-state      # SecureBoot enabled

check.q: Where does UEFI look for bootloaders?
check.a: In .efi files on the EFI System Partition (a FAT-formatted GPT partition), referenced by NVRAM boot entries.

stage-2-the-bootloader-grub.core: GRUB 2 presents a menu, reads its config (grub.cfg, generated from /etc/default/grub and /etc/grub.d by update-grub or grub2-mkconfig), loads the chosen kernel image (vmlinuz) and initramfs into memory, and passes the kernel command line: root=UUID=..., console=ttyS0, quiet, plus tuning parameters. You can edit entries at boot (e) to fix problems, for example adding systemd.unit=rescue.target or init=/bin/bash.

first_principles.problem: A wrong root= UUID after a disk change leaves the system unable to find its root filesystem.
truths: The command line configures the kernel.
derivation: Edit entries at boot with **e** for rescue.

analogy.title: A stage manager handing the lead actor the script
analogy.story: GRUB chooses which actor (kernel) goes on, gives them their opening lines (command line) and their props (initramfs).
analogy.breaks: Actors improvise; kernels follow the command line literally.

code.text:
sed -i 's/^GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX="/&console=ttyS0,115200 transparent_hugepage=madvise /' /etc/default/grub
update-grub           # Debian/Ubuntu
# grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg   # RHEL
cat /proc/cmdline     # after reboot

check.q: Why shouldn't you edit grub.cfg directly?
check.a: It's regenerated from /etc/default/grub and /etc/grub.d by update-grub/grub2-mkconfig, overwriting manual edits.

stage-3-the-kernel-initializes.core: The kernel decompresses itself, sets up memory management and page tables, brings up CPUs (SMP), initialises the scheduler, timers and interrupts, probes built-in drivers, parses the command line, then mounts the initramfs as a temporary root and executes /init. dmesg records every step. Kernel panics here usually mean missing storage drivers, bad parameters, hardware faults or incompatible kernel builds.

first_principles.problem: After a kernel upgrade the server panics with 'VFS: Unable to mount root fs on unknown-block(0,0)'.
truths: The kernel must initialise hardware first.
Drivers may be built-in or modules.

analogy.title: A new building manager's first morning
analogy.story: Turn on power, check the lifts, wake the security systems and confirm the floors exist before letting anyone in.
analogy.breaks: Managers can call for help; a panicked kernel just stops.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Missing NVMe driver added; boots again.

code.text:
# boot previous kernel from GRUB menu, then:
journalctl -k -b -1 | tail -40       # previous boot's kernel log
lsinitrd /boot/initramfs-$(uname -r).img | grep -E 'nvme|virtio'
dracut -f --kver 6.8.0-45-generic    # rebuild initramfs with drivers

check.q: What does 'VFS: Unable to mount root fs on unknown-block(0,0)' usually mean?
check.a: The kernel can't find the root device, often because the initramfs is missing or lacks the storage driver, or root= is wrong.

stage-4-the-initramfs-trick.core: The real root filesystem may sit on NVMe, LVM, RAID, LUKS encryption, iSCSI or the network, which needs drivers and userspace tools the kernel doesn't have built in. The initramfs is a small compressed cpio archive loaded into RAM as a temporary root. Its /init (dracut, initramfs-tools or systemd in the initrd) loads modules, assembles RAID or LVM, unlocks LUKS, mounts the real root, then switch_roots into it. When it fails you get an emergency shell.

first_principles.problem: A server with LUKS-encrypted root drops to an emergency shell after the disk controller changes.
truths: The kernel can't include every driver.
A temporary RAM root bridges the gap.

analogy.title: A scaffold used to reach the real building's entrance
analogy.story: A temporary structure lets you get in; once inside, it's taken down.
analogy.breaks: Scaffolds are built on-site; initramfs must be prebuilt with the right tools.

code.text:
# at boot: add rd.break to kernel cmdline to stop before switch_root
lsinitrd | grep -E 'cryptsetup|megaraid'
dracut --add-drivers megaraid_sas -f
# Debian: echo megaraid_sas >> /etc/initramfs-tools/modules && update-initramfs -u

check.q: Why is an initramfs needed for systems with LUKS or LVM root filesystems?
check.a: Unlocking and assembling them needs userspace tools and drivers that must run before the real root can be mounted.

stage-5-pid-1-and-systemd.core: After switch_root, the kernel runs /sbin/init, which is systemd on most distros, as PID 1. systemd reads unit files, builds a dependency graph toward the default target (multi-user.target or graphical.target), starts units in parallel respecting dependencies, mounts filesystems from fstab, starts journald and udev, and reaps orphans. If PID 1 dies, the kernel panics. systemd-analyze shows where boot time goes.

first_principles.problem: Boot takes 90 seconds, and the team doesn't know which service is slow.

analogy.title: An orchestra conductor
analogy.story: They start each section when its cues are met, many playing at once, until the full piece is running.
analogy.breaks: Conductors can improvise; systemd follows unit definitions strictly.

code.text:
systemd-analyze
# Startup finished in 3.1s (kernel) + 4.2s (initrd) + 82.4s (userspace)
systemd-analyze critical-chain | head
# network-online.target @80.1s
#  └─NetworkManager-wait-online.service +78.9s
systemctl --failed

check.a: The kernel panics, since PID 1 is required to run the system and reap orphaned processes.
